I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment

When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

vignette: The capture began on a routine trawl shift when a foreign patrol vessel alongside theirs ordered the boat to surface. What followed was a series of damp holding cells and a long interrogation that stretched into days. He was held face-down on cold concrete, wrists bound behind him, forced to listen to muffled sobs from adjacent rooms while heavy boots paced and struck the metal walls. Through a ventilation shaft, a baby's cry cut through the air, sharp and relentless. He was stripped of his jacket, made to kneel with his shoulders exposed, and pushed to speak of routes and contacts he knew nothing of. The weight of it came from being pinned down, forced to break, unable to look away or close the distance. Elias was twenty-six years old, an American of European descent born to a Rhode Island fishing family that had later settled in a Pacific Northwest port town. When he returned to the coast, the world felt differently calibrated. He found himself unable to ride the public bus to the dock, no longer able to sit in the aisle with his shoulders hunched toward the windows. The confined rows, the sudden brakes, and the way the driver's voice cut through the engine hum replayed the weight of being cornered in a vehicle, trapped without a clear exit. He had come to believe that sitting upright or facing forward left him exposed, and began arriving two hours early, driving his own battered truck along the coastal road just to find a berth where his back could press against the reinforced bulkhead of the engine room. There, he listened for the particular shift in the house's floorboards or the click of a deadbolt, his head tilted toward the stairwell, tracking every footfall. In the galley and on the dock, his eyes moved past the ropes and nets to the hooks, the shears, the heavy winch handles, cataloguing what could be picked up and swung. He did not tell himself he was on guard; he simply noticed what could harm him, the way a sailor reads water. When the old footage surfaced, usually after a loud bang or a sudden silence, his shoulders would lock forward and his knees would draw up exactly as they had on that concrete floor. The familiar ache would flare in his forearms and ribs, the same bruised tender spots where the straps had dug in. His breath would catch, then harden into a hot, heavy pressure behind his sternum. He would press his palms flat against his thighs until the heat passed, certain that if he moved too quickly, the past would overtake him again. He did not describe it as a flashback. He called it remembering, and when the images returned, his jaw would set so tight it ached, a raw, consuming anger rising like a tide he had no channel for. Over the months, the routes he walked shrank. He stopped taking the bus, walked instead, and when his wife, Mara, began crying after a family call or when she pressed him about his sleepless nights, he felt that same hollow, exposed dread, the kind that came from being pushed past his limits, and he would turn off the radio, step onto the deck, and let the distance widen. He told himself it was better to keep the quiet, to not let her see him unravel, but the silence became a wall between their bed and the bunk. He worked, mended nets, and kept the engine running, but the hours stretched longer, the checks of the cabin more frequent. A child's laugh from a passing stroller on a supply run still pulled his gaze downward, his breath catching until the sound faded. Now, Elias sits in a clinic waiting room with his boots still damp from the morning tide. He has angled his chair so the wall supports his spine, one hand resting near the heavy door handle, the other scanning the reception desk for anything that looks like it could be used to pry or cut. He is here because Mara packed his bag, because the silence at home has grown too heavy to carry alone. He hopes someone can help him sleep without waking at the first footstep on the stairs, and what frightens him most is that the calm might slip away again, that he will never stop bracing for the next room to open.
